passage:
Dear Indu,

I am writing from Melbourne, where I came for a conference and to stay with Nisha, my old college friend. Nisha lives alone, pays for a home carer for her mother, and visits her only twice a year. At first I found it lonely: a quiet flat, dinner for one, and I kept thinking of our house with five people talking at once. But when Nisha talks about her work and how nobody plans her weekends for her, her face lights up. She told me the distance is the price of the life she chose, and some days she is not sure it is a fair price. I still cannot imagine living like that. I will try not to read her life as cold.

Tell Mummy I will call on Sunday.

Alka

qa.q: Where is Alka writing the letter from?
qa.a: Alka is writing from Melbourne.

qa.q: What did Alka feel about Nisha's quiet flat at first?
qa.a: Alka found it lonely, missing the noisy house with five people talking at once.

qa.q: What could Alka do to see Nisha's life more fairly?
qa.a: Alka could keep listening to Nisha's own reasons and notice the parts that give Nisha joy, instead of reading the quiet as coldness.

qa.q: How does Nisha herself see her way of life?
qa.a: Nisha values planning her own weekends and calls the distance the price of the life she chose, though some days she is not sure it is a fair price.

grounding: A person from a close family culture finds friends' solitary life abroad lonely, yet sees the freedom those friends value.

Thanks for having me, Sachin. I'm Chandrika. You asked what surprised me on my trip to Toronto. I went to visit Marcus, a friend from my exchange year. His father lives back in Ohio with a paid home helper, and Marcus sees him twice a year. I was ready to feel sorry for him: a small flat, takeaway dinner, an empty calendar on Sundays. Where I come from, we would have called that lonely, and honestly, in the first two days I did.
Then I saw him on a video call with his father at eight sharp, laughing about a crossword. He told me he loves that no one decides his weekends, and that he still worries some nights about being far away. I went home still preferring my noisy family dinners. But I stopped calling his life cold.

On the second Sunday of the month Usha took the train from her Pune flat to her parents' house. Over lunch her aunt said, "Why live alone when there's a room here?" Usha smiled and passed the salad. "Because I like my own place. But look at our whiteboard." On it, in Usha's handwriting: Usha pays the monthly grocery order and calls on odd days. Her brother Chaitanya handles the society meetings and bank visits and calls on even days. Wednesday evenings were Usha's pottery class, and nobody phoned then unless it mattered.
"We agreed this in March," Usha said. "If it gets heavy for anyone, we change it." Her father tapped the board and nodded, as if it were a contract everyone had signed.

Something has been bothering me at home. Papa keeps a steel cupboard locked, and when a relative phones about "the land", Mum switches off the TV and takes the call in the other room. Thomas
